utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please call the case, if it's a case. It's not a case -- in fact, it's not going to be called as a case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Proceedings in the matter regarding the report by Mr. Ukropina dated 14th June 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, this is today more of a formality than anything else, but I want to make sure that you are able to follow these proceedings in a language that you can understand. And so far could you hear me in a language that you could understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and you may sit down. Appearances for Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: James Shellow, Milwaukee Wisconsin. With me at counsel table is Ms. Maglov and Ms. Jetovic, who with leave of the court will act as an interpreter should it be necessary for me to confer with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. And welcome to this Tribunal and good afternoon to you. I understand also that there is the amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dejan Ukropina, attorney amicus curiae on the basis of the registrar's decision dated the 26th of April 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, and I see there is a representation from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in a hearing which is not a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're here at Your Honours' invitation, or rather, acquiescence in the fact that we can be here to at least listen to the proceedings. Joanna Korner, together with Ann Sutherland, and no case manager today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. And that means we can proceed. And we'll start with a very short introduction from the Bench to address more or less the parameters of today's hearing. The hearing has been convened primarily because there was an ad hoc request from Ms. Maglov herself for such a hearing, and the request being presented to us by Mr. Ackerman in one of the sittings dating back about a fortnight ago or three weeks ago, a request which the Trial Chamber has absolutely no hesitation at all in acceding to, because we feel, as we actually expressed ourselves already on more than one occasion, that this is a matter of a right which Ms. Maglov has once that a report has been filed -- has been filed. It also means that what is expected from you, Mr. Shellow, in particular is to address whatever you think needs to be addressed but arising from the report of Mr. Ukropina. And I need to make it clear that we do not have contempt proceedings here that we are dealing with and that we will not be dealing with matters which could be related intimately to contempt proceedings if there will ever be contempt proceedings but only with regard to matters arising from this report which would help us reach an appropriate decision. In other words, these were two. We could have given Ms. Maglov an opportunity to file written arguments arising from the report or give a hearing. And since there was a specific request or a preference shown for a hearing, we decided to give a hearing. It doesn't mean to say that we will expose everyone here to -- to go beyond what is strictly pertinent to the report and invade territories which could or could not arise in the future. As far as the other reason/purpose for this hearing today, is to give the opportunity also to Ms. Maglov and her attorney to put questions to Mr. Ukropina arising out of the report that he has filed and also providing us, the three Judges up here, with the opportunity of putting questions to Mr. Ukropina which might help, perhaps clarify certain points that one or more of us needs to be clarified. It's needless to say that we made it also clear that this was a hearing which could be of interest both to the accused Brdjanin and to the Prosecution -- or to the Office of the Prosecutor. The reason being is that we opted for the appointment of an amicus curiae rather than the prosecutor to investigate the matter. So that goes without saying that there may or may not be an interest for the Office of the Prosecutor to go into the matter of this report. We will not insist on either the defendant or the Prosecution to involve themselves in today's hearing. But if they wish to do so, they are at liberty to do so. With that, I think I will give you the floor, Mr. Shellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is an honour and a privilege to appear before this Tribunal in these historic proceedings. As I indicated, I am a practicing attorney. I have devoted full time to the practice of criminal defence law throughout the United States for some 41 years. My office is in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The submission I make today will be based exclusively upon the report prepared by the amicus curiae and certain representations made in open court by the prosecutor which are relevant to an understanding of the report by the amicus. In one instance in which statements taken by the amicus or a statement taken by the amicus contains an answer or an assertion that is contradicted by another statement of another witness taken by the amicus, I will assume for the purpose of this submission the correctness of the version which favours the Prosecution. The facts, I believe, as developed from the amicus and his report and as I say, by representation on one occasion by the Prosecution, are relatively straight forward and largely uncontroverted. In September and December in 2001, Ms. Maglov, accompanied by an attorney, Mr. Peric, interviewed a witness in Kotor Varos. They interviewed the witness in September, and at that time the witness was asked whether or not he would give a statement or testify for the defendant, and the witness said he would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry to interrupt my learned friend. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner. Microphone, please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Although he's being careful not to mention the name of the witness, the circumstances he's already outlining may disclose the identity of the witness. This is in open session at, I understand, the request of Mr. Shellow. If he's going to give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is an open witness -- an open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because no request has been forthcoming to have it in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't -- it's my fault, Your Honour. Had I known that Mr. Shellow was going to go into this, I would have asked for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can keep it open session and I can invite Mr. Shellow to avoid mentioning names. We know who the three persons involved are, as your client and two other persons, one of -- one of whom appears only on the scene in December. So you could restrict yourself to indicating -- to referring them -- to them by Mr. 1 -- Mr. X and Mr. Y, Mr. Y being the last person you mentioned and who came to the scene -- appeared on the scene in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that way we will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And Your Honour, can I ask for the transcript to be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And 22 -- 20 to 22 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please take care that the redaction is put in place. I thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's actually Ms. Sutherland as usual who Your Honours should thank. She reminded me of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: As do I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Shellow, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: The -- Ms. Maglov and Mr. X then accompanied Mr. Y to the office of the witness. Prior to that and in September it should be noted that when Ms. Maglov and her fellow attorney arrived in Kotor Varos, they presented their identification to the chief of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to mention him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is mentioned in the report. We know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: And they identified themselves as being members of the Defence team representing Mr. Brdjanin. It was he through his secretary that escorted Ms. Maglov and her colleague to the office of the witness. It was he who suggested that that witness and another might be helpful to the inquiry that Ms. Maglov and her colleague were making. Now, as I say, in September Ms. Maglov and her colleague questioned the witness about the events that took place in Kotor Varos in 1992 and before and later. And during this time and prior to questioning about these events they identified themselves to the witness and identified that they were on the Defence team of Mr. Brdjanin. At some point they asked the witness whether or not the witness would be will be to give a statement or to testify on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin, and the witness declined. Thereafter, as I say, in December -- in December, Ms. Maglov and her colleague were again in Kotor Varos, and at that time Mr. Z expressed an interest in speaking with the witness, and the three of them proceeded to the witness's office. On that occasion there is nothing in the record to show whether Ms. Maglov and her colleague reintroduced themselves to the witness, but it seems it would be unlikely since they had done so three months before. They asked no substantive questions of the witness. The witness and Mr. Z recounted their experiences since they had last met, and at one point, according to Mr. Z, Ms. Maglov again asked the witness, inquired of the witness, whether the witness would be willing to give a statement or testify on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin, and the witness said no. That's the substance of the facts in the case. It is -- it is clear from the statement of the witness and from the statement of Mr. Z that the witness was uncomfortable, that the witness felt insecure, that the witness felt some anxiety, that the witness -- the witness may have felt -- we don't know. We don't know what occasioned this. It may have been the question by Ms. Maglov. It may have been the circumstances. It may have been the presence of Mr. Z. It may have been the concern of the witness that the statement he had previously given to the Prosecution, that is, at some point -- it may have been that that statement wasn't correct and he was concerned about it and concerned about being cross-examined over it. We just don't know. We do know it is uncontroverted that in September neither Ms. Maglov nor her colleague had any knowledge that the witness was on the Prosecution's witness list. Between September and December they read the statement of the witness, knew that the witness was on the Prosecutor's list, and knew he was on the list when it's asserted that Ms. Maglov asked him the second time whether he'd be willing to also give a statement for the Defence. As I read the report of the amicus, the amicus assumes that the witness had a protected status. According to the representations made in court by the Prosecution on two days, the witness did not have a protected status, the witness at some point had asked to have a protected status, and the Prosecutor represented to the Court that no witness from that municipality had been given protected status, and that was as of April 2002. The Prosecutor further represented that it was the practice of the office not to grant or not to seek protected status for a witness until they could do so for every witness from the municipality, and that hadn't been done for the municipality in which this witness would have been included. Now, from these facts the amicus concludes that Ms. Maglov may have done something improper. He suggests that if the witness -- if Ms. Maglov knew of the protected status of the witness, that asking the question a second time might be considered some form of pressure or intimidation. Well, first of all, the witness did not have a protected status, so there's no way in the world that Ms. Maglov could have known that he did. Second of all, there is nothing improper about asking a witness the same question more than once, particularly if you believe circumstances have changed since the question was first asked. That is, in September Ms. Maglov and her colleague did not know that the witness had agreed to give a statement for the Prosecution. After learning that, I think it was perfectly reasonable to ask a second time, "Are you willing to give a statement to the Defence also?" The witness's attitude towards giving statements may well have changed in the intervening three months or Ms. Maglov may have believed that they might have changed. In any event, the amicus has also suggested in his report that attorneys under the Code of Professional Conduct for Defence lawyers and under Rule 77 of this Tribunal are responsible not only for what they know but for what they should have known. And I will address that later in this submission. But at this juncture and in this introduction I would merely state that I do not believe that position is tenable, nor is it supported by such case law as I have found since I agreed to this representation. I agreed to represent Ms. Maglov pro bono because the issues that are raised by the amicus are important not only to Ms. Maglov but to the entire Defence bar of this Tribunal, and in particular the interpretation of the amicus that a lawyer may be in contempt for what he should have known but did not know is a position that would have perhaps tragic consequences in the representation of persons who are accused before this Tribunal, for it would make lawyers, even the most experienced ones, wary in conducting interviews with potential witnesses. It would put them on notice that they will be responsible for whatever some tribunal or prosecutor concludes they should have known but did not know. And as I say, I will address that later and the authorities in support of it. The question of the vigour, imagination, creativity, and tenaciousness of Defence counsel was addressed by Judge Hunt in pre-trial rulings in this cause. And with all deference to the amicus, Your Honour, I believe that if the amicus had placed the conduct of Ms. Maglov in the context of Judge Hunt's rulings, the report would have been quite different. Finally - finally -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to be more specific in this context, Mr. Shellow, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which decisions by Judge Hunt --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you are referring to in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Yes. May I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while Mr. Shellow is looking for the judgement, can I just say this -- and so that Your Honours can make a decision. Your Honour, what Mr. Shellow is actually doing is going into the facts of this -- this matter. He has made various assertions which on the face of it are not right, and there are factual -- Your Honour, I know, but this is my -- my concern. This is really a matter for Your Honours having decided on the basis of the report by Mr. Ukropina whether this is a matter to refer or not. But I can see this developing into a discussion, at the very least, on the facts as revealed by this report. And that's the real problem, I raise before Your Honour. And I'm simply mentioning it now so that Your Honour has this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We take note of it. But let's proceed for the time being, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: In response to the Court's question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: It is the decision of July 3, 2000. And I would invite the attention of the Tribunal in particular to pages 14 and 15 of that decision. Now, the last point I wish to make in this introduction is that in reviewing the Rule 77 of this Tribunal, the rule that addresses contempt, and in reviewing the Code of Professional Conduct for Defence lawyers, and in particular the provisions identified by the amicus as potentially violated, which are 5(A) and (D) as I recall, the admonitions of the code and its provisions are so vague and uncertain that to apply them to whether or not a violation can be constructed from one who asks a question on two occasions of a witness renders those provisions of the code and the rule insofar as it would adopt those provisions of the code void for vagueness. That is, no reasonable person would be on notice in reading those provisions, that it would cover the conduct in which it is alleged Ms. Maglov engaged. That is, if this Court were to construe Rule 77 as it incorporates the Code of Professional Conduct for Defence lawyers to apply to the conduct in which it is alleged Ms. Maglov engaged, then those provisions as applied in the judgement of counsel and upon the cases counsel will invite to the attention of the Tribunal void for vagueness. Now, as the Tribunal is aware, contempt is an awesome power. It is a power common law courts have held for hundreds and hundreds of years. In the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a lecture that I made this morning, which I -- we discussed at length, especially considering that the -- my two colleagues come from jurisdictions where the concept of contempt is not exactly completely alien but more or less alien. In my jurisdiction, it's not alien at all. We resort to it. I have resorted to it on several occasions. In the past 20 years we have been more hesitant because of the impact of the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, and the concern that there is that contempt issues are better looked upon now and addressed in the lights of certain modern developments. But anyway, go ahead, Mr. Shellow. But we don't need a lecture on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to avoid giving us a lecture on -- on how awesome -- how desirable or undesirable the institute of contempt is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: I recall the Court's inviting attention of counsel to the treatise by Alfred -- Lord Denning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: And it would be bringing, as they say, coals to Newcastle, for me to engage in some sort of professorial discussion concerning the significance of contempt. It seems to me though that in the context of a contempt proceeding against a lawyer involved in the defence of a criminal case, unlike a contempt proceeding brought against a lawyer who publicly maligns a judge or who makes a public statement to the newspaper in violation of some court order, the impact of contempt, even the proceeding in contempt, will chill not only that lawyer's representation and make it less effective, but it will send a message to all defence lawyers that they must be cautious, that they should be prudent rather than vigorous, that they should be fearful rather than courageous. And so the threat of contempt impacts not only upon the lawyer who is the alleged contemner but upon the client whose representation will be and may be impaired. So I invited the attention in the introduction to the representation by the Prosecutor that the witness did not have a protected status as of April 2002. And in particular, I would now invite the Court's attention to the transcript of 8 April 2002, at page 3826, in which the Prosecutor stated he asked for full protection. And then on the following day at transcript pages 3924 through 3926 the Prosecutor stated that an application for protected status had not been made for the witness nor for any witness in the municipality. The statement of Judge Hunt to which I referred at pages 14 and 15 of the 3 July 2000 was as follows: "The Appeals Chamber has placed a firm obligation upon those representing an accused person to make proper inquiries as to what evidence is available in that person's defence. Some of the Prosecution witnesses are likely to be of such importance that it will be necessary for at least the final stage of the investigation into those witnesses to be done by counsel who is appearing -- who is to appear for the accused at trial. That is obvious to anyone with experience of criminal trials." And that says not that lawyers have the power to interview witnesses but that they have the obligation to interview them and they have an obligation to interview Prosecution witnesses, whether they are on the Prosecutor's list of witnesses or not, and indeed whether they are protected witnesses or not. Now, as far as the witness is concerned, the witness had no recollection of being interviewed on any occasion except the occasion when Ms. Maglov, her colleague, and Mr. Z were present. That would make it the December interview. And I believe if the Court reviews the statement of the witness, in the light of the uncontroverted facts set forth in the statements of Ms. Maglov and her colleague, the Court will reach the conclusion that what the witness has done is to have taken the questions asked of him in September and placed them as though they were asked in December; that is, that he has collapsed the two contacts that he had with Ms. Maglov into one. But that is something that this Chamber is as capable of assessing as counsel is. Ms. Maglov's colleague gave the statement to the amicus. Referring to the September meeting, "He, the witness, showed up." I'm reading from page 8633, page 8631, and 8632. "He, the witness, showed up. We shook hands and introduced ourselves as attorneys from Mr. Brdjanin's Defence team. Then he told us almost at the end of the conversation that he was contacted by someone from the Tribunal and he gave the statement. Also he would not like to testify. Until that moment we were not aware he was in contact with representatives of the Prosecution, and the statement was not given to us before. We have exchanged cards and left." He continues: "I think his statement was given to us between those two meetings." That would be the meetings in September and December. "That he is a witness. I was aware during the first meeting when he told us he had contacts with someone from the Tribunal. I understood that he had talked to investigators. But we were not given his statement from the Prosecution and not aware he is a witness, nor that the Prosecution is planning to include him as a witness." I believe when this Tribunal reads the statements of Ms. Maglov, her colleague who accompanied her both in September and December, and Mr. Z that these statements are largely consistent. Each remembers obviously some things that the others didn't. And I believe that in reading these three statements, the Court will reach an understanding of what transpired on those two occasions and would conclude, as counsel did, that Ms. Maglov and her colleague did absolutely nothing wrong. They acted in the highest traditions of the Defence bar. They certainly did not intimidate, threaten, coerce, bribe, or attempt to influence anyone's testimony. At the September meeting the amicus reports that the witness stated that they asked him wasn't it -- they asked him a question about who had responsibility for the events or some of the events in Kotor Varos and was it perhaps a divided responsibility. And he said no. Or at least as I read his statement, he's saying no. And yet, that's precisely the question every member of this Tribunal would ask: Or a defendant is charged not with committing acts but with soliciting others; or commanding others; or conspiring with others; or aiding and abetting others to commit acts. And so I turn to the charges, and charges in only a very loose sense. The Prosecutor put forth essentially suggestions for inquiry. Upon those suggestions for inquiry the registrar raised the following issues -- but before I go to the registrar's issues, perhaps I ought to briefly dwell on the Prosecutor's inquiries that prompted the Registrar's issues. And these -- these appear in the report of the amicus, of course: How the Defence team learned the whereabouts of the witness. Obviously the Prosecutor was concerned. If the witness was someone who himself was concerned, the Prosecutor was concerned how did they find him. Well, we now know how they found him. They didn't find him by rifling the Prosecution's files or tapping the Prosecutor's phone, or finding an informant in the Prosecutor's office. No, they found him in exactly the same way any defence lawyer would have found a witness. They went to somebody whom they felt might know witnesses in the area who could help and they asked him, "Who do you know?" And he gave the name of two witnesses, one of them being the witness under consideration. Second of all, the question is whether Ms. Maglov and her colleague identified themselves as members of Mr. Brdjanin's Defence team. They say they did in the September meeting. The discussion of the December meeting is silent on that, but it would seem to be a -- a pointless introduction were they to reintroduce themselves every time they encounter a witness. Further, as a sort of aside to that whole question of did they introduce themselves or didn't they, the Code of Professional Conduct for Defence lawyers is silent on this issue; that is, it does not address whether witnesses should be told who their interviewer is and what his role is. It probably is a good practice to do so. It certainly is a good judgement to do so. It's the decent thing to do. But I don't think you have to do it twice. And the code doesn't require that you do it even once. The third thing that the Prosecutor raised, the third question, whether Ms. Maglov influenced or attempted to influence the witness not to testify about matters which he knew. There's nothing, of course, in the report of the amicus or the statement of the witness that that ever occurred. The witness was asked whether there was a divided responsibility, as I indicated, and the witness was never said -- the witness was never told, "Look, if there wasn't a divided responsibility, I want you to testify that there was." He was never encouraged to commit perjury. He was never threatened. He was never coerced. Then based upon these inquiries by the Prosecution, the Registry and its Registrar asked the following -- that the following questions be addressed by the amicus: The reason behind Ms. Maglov's visit to the witness. Well, the reason behind her visit to the witness is the reason behind anyone's visit to a witness. You go to a witness to find out what the witness knows and whether the witness can help you. Secondly, whether the -- at the commencement of the visit, Ms. Maglov identified herself and her role. It's uncontroverted that they did so when they first interviewed the witness in September. And as I say, perhaps it would have been gracious to do it a second time. Perhaps it would have been good manners to do it a second time. It would be the patrician thing to do. But it's hardly mandated by the code, the rule, or the code of professional responsibility for lawyers. The third issue raised by the Registrar was whether Ms. Maglov or anyone accompanying her committed any act in violation of Rule 77. And I've already addressed that there was no violation of this rule, nothing in the question that was asked of the witness on the two occasions when it was asked intimidated the witness. It was a perfectly neutral question asked in a neutral way. It didn't suggest that bad things would happen to the witness if the witness testified for the Prosecution or refused to testify for the Defence. It just simply asked: Would you be willing to do it? And the witness reiterated his answer that he gave in September, in which he said no. Defence lawyers have a right to ask the question. They have a right to ask it once. They have a right to ask it twice. They have a right to ask it as many times as they feel is necessary in the case where there is a witness where the circumstances may have changed. And lastly, whether any other aspect of Ms. Maglov's contact with the witness is relevant to her appointment considering the directive on assignment. And the amicus concludes there was no such relevance. I suggest to the Court -- excuse me, to the Tribunal, most respectfully, that while this is a preliminary proceeding to give the Court the opportunity to hear Ms. Maglov by counsel give his views of what the amicus report shows that it also would be appropriate for this Tribunal to make at the conclusion - at the conclusion of these preliminary proceedings - to make findings of fact and conclusions law. And I would ask the Tribunal to consider the following as findings of fact supported by the report of the amicus and by the transcript pages to which I referred the representations of the Prosecution: 1: The reason Ms. Maglov and her colleague went to Kotor Varos in September 2001 was primarily to talk with a man who's been identified as the chief of the municipality and to seek his help in locating persons who had been on the Crisis Staff. Prior to speaking with the chief -- the President of the Municipality, the chief of the municipality, neither Ms. Maglov nor her colleague had any knowledge of the existence of the witness. 3: Ms. Maglov and her colleague identified themselves to the President of the Municipality as members of the Brdjanin Defence team. 4: The President of the Municipality suggested that Ms. Maglov and her colleague might wish to speak to two witnesses and who might be able to provide evidence. One of the persons identified by the chief of the municipality was the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: 7: After discussing unrelated social matters with the witness and placing him at his ease, Ms. Maglov and Mr. Peric identified themselves as members of the Brdjanin Defence team. 8: At the time of their September conversation with the witness, neither Ms. Maglov nor her colleague had knowledge that the witness was listed as a Prosecution witness. 9: During their September conversation with the witness, Ms. Maglov and her colleague learned that the witness had been interviewed by someone from the Tribunal. 10: Ms. Maglov and her colleague assumed in September that the witness was not listed as a Prosecution witness because they had not read and did not believe that they had received the witness statement. 11: Prior to the September interview, Ms. Maglov and her colleague had not seen a statement of the witness and on that basis assumed that the witness had been interviewed by an investigator and was not on the Prosecutor's list of witnesses; that is, in the September interview. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Shellow, may I ask you to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: 12: -- Incidentally, Your Honour, in that context, with leave of the Court, I would be pleased to file with your clerk the outline -- or with your reporter the outline from which I am reading and which will have the citation to some of the cases to which I would invite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would certainly be most helpful, Mr Shellow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Thank you. And I do have leave of the Court -- of the Tribunal to do this. And I apologise for referring to the Tribunal as a Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make sure that when you do so, there is a copy made available to -- not just for the Tribunal but also for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. May I repeat 11. In the September interview, Ms. Maglov and her colleague had not seen a statement of the witness and when they learned that the witness had been interviewed they assumed it was by an investigator, and that is why the name was not on the Prosecutor's list of witnesses. The witness had no specific recollection of the September meeting and was -- and therefore confused what occurred at that meeting with what occurred at the meeting of December 2001. In September, when the witness was advised of the role of Ms. Maglov and her colleague, the witness stated that he did not wish to give a statement to Defence counsel and would not state that there had been a divided responsibility for the occurrences with which the defendant is charged. Between September and December, Ms. Maglov and Mr. Peric read the statement of the witness and learned that the witness would testify for the Prosecution. 15: Ms. Maglov and her colleague had no reason to believe that the witness had a protected status because personal identifying information had not been redacted from the statement -- from his statement. 16: The witness did not have the status of a protected witness in September and December 2001. 17: During the December contact with Ms. Maglov, her colleague, and Mr. Z, the only question asked of the witness was whether he would testify for -- whether he would testify for the Defence, and the witness reiterated that he would not give a statement to Defence counsel. 18: In neither the September nor December conversations with the witness did either Ms. Maglov or her colleague threaten or attempt to intimidate the witness, nor did they in the December conversation attempt to have the witness contradict what the witness had stated to the Prosecutor. 19: During the December meeting the witness was anxious and fearful that his identity as a Prosecution witness would become known to the community in which he lived and worked. 20: During the December conversation, the witness felt that because he was asked a second time to give a statement to Defence attorneys after he declined their first request, he was being pressured. Based upon the law I will discuss, I ask for the following conclusions of law: 1: Neither Ms. Maglov nor her colleague attempted to pressure or intimidate a witness to change a statement he had given the Prosecution. 2: Neither Ms. Maglov nor Mr. Peric failed to identify themselves in and their role to the witness. 3: Neither Ms. Maglov nor Mr. Peric attempted to obstruct the administration of justice by the Tribunal. 4: Neither Ms. Maglov nor Mr. Peric violated the provisions of the Code of Conduct for Defence lawyers or the Rules of this Tribunal. 5: The subjective feelings of anxiety, fearfulness, insecurity, and pressure by a witness do not evidence intimidation unless they are shown to be the intended result of statements or conducts of counsel. 6: It is proper for Defence counsel to interview Prosecution witnesses, including those upon whom has been conferred a protected status. The amicus opines that at page 8669 -- that if Ms. Maglov were aware of the status of the witness, the reasons behind the visit -- the reason behind this visit could be -- could be understand as intimidation. Well, it is a confusing statement at best. It is difficult to discern what the amicus means by "the status of the witness." Does he mean the protected status of the witness? If that's what he means, he's in error. The witness didn't have a protected status. The witness was not a protected status witness. If he means that the status of the witness was someone on the Prosecutor's witness list, it's absurd. I would ask the Court to listen to it again. If Ms. Maglov was aware of the status of the witness, the reason behind the visits could be understand as intimidation. That is, if they knew he was a Prosecution witness who had already given a statement and then you ask him to give a statement for the Defence, that this constitutes intimidation? If it is, we should all go out of business and write wills for a living. I submit --

utterances.text: The amicus goes on: In the context of this statement, if Ms. Maglov and Mr. Peric were aware or should have been aware of the status of the witness, Article 5(A) and (D) of the Code of Professional Conduct were violated. I read to this Tribunal the provisions of Article 5(A) and (D): "In providing representation to a client, counsel must: A, act with competence, skill, care, honesty, and loyalty." I submit that if that provision is construed to bar an attorney from either questioning someone on a Prosecutor's witness list or bar an attorney from asking the same question twice, that the effective representation of counsel in this -- before this Tribunal will be impaired. And if the code is construed to apply -- to questioning with Prosecution witness and asking the same question twice, then that provision of the code does not place an attorney on notice as to what conduct is prohibited and it's void for vagueness. Secondly, provision D, the other one upon which the amicus relies: "In providing representation to a client, counsel must preserve their own integrity and that of the legal profession as a whole." The integrity of the lawyer defending a client in a serious criminal case requires that he conduct himself vigorously, imaginatively, creatively, tenaciously. And if that representation requires in his judgement that he be asked -- that the witness be asked the same question twice, then so be it. That is the way the integrity of the profession is maintained. It is not maintained by those who represent their client and are meek and fearful and concerned that some overreaching prosecutor will attempt to haul them into a tribunal on contempt charges. As I indicated, there is no requirement in this code, either in the provisions that were read and to which the amicus invited our attention or an other provision, which recites that counsel has an obligation to identify himself before interviewing a witness. As I indicated -- I think it's good manners. I think it reflects well upon us. I think it's the gracious thing to do, as it is the gracious thing to do, to introduce yourself to anyone you encounter and wish to talk to. But the Code of Professional Conduct did not incorporate Amy Vanderbilt's book on etiquette. And now to the law, Your Honours. I apologise to the Tribunal. My experience with international law is not great. I have briefly practiced in Canada and in Mexico, but the majority of my practice - the almost exclusive practice - is within the United States and perhaps for the last couple of decades primarily in the Federal courts in the United States. I might note that if -- if within the general defence of criminal cases there is a specialty, I have probably devoted my time more to the defence of cases where defendants were charged with a vicarious liability for the acts of others. And so I find myself defending conspiracy cases, cases in which persons were charged with having acted in concert under statutes that prohibit that, cases involving aiding and abetting, liability. It is a long time ago, but in 1960 -- 1960 while I was in law school -- 1960 or in 1959 I wrote my first article on conspiracy law and have been following it, I think diligently, ever since. Now, with my apologies for not being able to cite cases from other countries, I invite the attention to the law that I know. It is axiomatic certainly in the United States that a person should not be required to guess at his peril as to the meaning of a statute or code provision which imposes serious penal consequences. For the past 65 years that principle has been expressed in the courts of United States. It was first expressed in 1926 by Mr. Justice Sutherland in Connally versus General Construction Company. The citation is in the outline. But Justice Sutherland wrote: "A penal statute which either forbids or requires the doing of an act in terms so vague that men of common intelligence must necessarily guess at its meaning and differ as to its application is void for vagueness." I cite the Court to other Supreme Court cases that have held the same, but I note that when I looked in the -- when I did a database search, over 400 opinions of Federal Courts have quoted that language since it was first expressed by Mr. Justice Sutherland. And so I ask the Court that if it believes, if it concludes that the provisions of Rule 77 and the provisions of the code of conduct encompass the conduct, apply to the conduct in which it is alleged Ms. Maglov was engaged with this witness, that those provisions of the code and that application of the rules give no notice and are void for that reason. For if you read the provisions of the code, in the context of Rule 77, it can hardly be said that an attorney would be on notice, that he could not interview a Prosecution witness, and that he could not ask such a witness the same question twice. The more interesting question, from -- at least certainly from an academic point of view is: How does a Tribunal such as this address the validity of a code? In this context, I wish to invite the Court's attention to the case of in re Frank Oliver, attorney. And the citation is in my outline. There was a trial in Chicago, a trial that created a great deal of publicity and about which there was a great deal of concern called the trial of the Chicago Seven. It was a group of persons who had demonstrated during the democratic convention in Chicago. The trial was heard by Judge Julias Hoffman of the Federal Court in Chicago. For the first time, certainly in that district, metal detectors were placed such that anyone entering the courthouse would be required to go through the metal detector. Mr. Oliver, a senior member of the bar of that court and perhaps its most distinguished member, drafted a letter to the executive board of judges of the Federal District Court, saying in substance as follows: "The undersigned senior members of your bar observe the metal detectors and are concerned. It may be that jurors passing through those metal detectors will believe that the republic is threatened and will convict people whom they otherwise would acquit because of such fear. On the other hand, jurors going through may be so annoyed by the invasion of their privacy that they would acquit persons which on other circumstances they might convict." He said, we do not know and we offer the services of the undersigned to discuss this with the Court, very truly yours, signed by 30 lawyers, including myself. Mr. Oliver sent this letter to the Court. The Court gave it to its clerk. The clerk file-stamped and it put a case number on it. Mr. Oliver gave a statement to the press, which basically is what I just explained to you. This is the petition that was filed and this is why it was filed. The Court convened on its own order to show cause why Mr. Oliver should not be held in contempt for violating that rule of court that says there shall be no comment on pending litigation and the Court defined the letter as pending litigation because it was given a file stamp. I defended Mr. Oliver. He said his conduct was protected by the first amendment and that's all. He said he knew about the code of professional responsibility, he knew about the Illinois rules of ethics, he now about the American Bar Association Code of Professional Conduct, and he knew all these things at the time he made this statement and that his statement was protected. The Prosecutor did not attempt to defend the code. The prosecutor said he has no right to challenge it. The Trial Court held Mr. Oliver in contempt and said it would reprimand him and if he ever did it again, there would be serious consequences. We appealed to the Unites States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit which reversed the conviction for contempt. But in the course of it observed the following in connection with the prosecutor's argument: "There is a fundamental distinction --" this is Chief Jerry Swagart [phoen] writing for the Court -- "There is a fundamental distinction between the functions of a court in its usual adjudicative role in which it is restricted to determining relative rights between parties, clearly subject to its jurisdiction based upon facts then made known to the Court, and the function of a court in an essentially legislative role in which it adopts broad rules perhaps having their greatest effect on parties not before it based on large facts that are largely anticipated. In this latter function, courts should be treated more like legislatures than courts in that their rule-making --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two positions appear in the report of the amicus really and in the colloquy with the Court engaged in by counsel in this cause. The Prosecutor asserted that Defence counsel was furnished with the witness's statement prior to the September interview. Ms. Maglov and her colleague assert that they had not read it prior to the September interview, they did not know of its existence, and they did not know of the existence of the witness nor his identity as a Prosecution witness. Ms. Maglov's colleague in his statement suggests a way of reconciling these -- these contrary positions and suggests that the process by which witness statements are first sent to lead counsel in Houston, then they're reduced to disks or scanned to disks or then the disks are provided to co-counsel in Banja Luka and that in this cumbersome process of data processing Ms. Maglov and her colleague had not started to read that group of material which included the statement of the witness and accordingly didn't know that the witness was on the Prosecution's witness list. The amicus takes the position that contempt could be considered - not that it should be brought, but that it could be considered - based upon the knowledge, based upon what they knew - and they claim they did not know - or what they should have known, even though they didn't have actual knowledge. And from the context, I -- I conclude that what the amicus is referring to is that they either knew or should have known that the witness was on the Prosecution's witness list. Well, there are two answers to that really: The first is it doesn't really make any difference if the witness was on the Prosecutor's list or not. They have a right and an obligation to interview that witness. But looking at it from the perspective of the amicus, who equates known and should have known, I most respectfully assert that the amicus is in error, that there is a difference in the law between what one knows and what one should have known, that contempt under the rules is only for knowing and wilful conduct, and that knowing conduct cannot be construed to be what someone should have known. In that -- in that context, I invite the Court's attention to United States versus Ladish Malting Company. Ladish Malting manufacturers malt that's used by the brewing industry, and they have a major plant and a workman went out on the fire escape to have a cigarette and the fire escape platform was rusted and he fell to -- the platform gave way and he fell to his death. The corporation was charged with a misdemeanour of really knowingly -- knowing an unsafe condition, doing nothing about it, and causing the death of the employee. The case was tried to a jury before a magistrate, and counsel repeatedly urged the magistrate that actual knowledge is required where a statute says "knowing." And the magistrate asserted with equal strength that no, no, the defendant corporation can be convicted if the prosecution proves it should have known of the unsafe condition of that fire escape. This colloquy with the Court concerning the meaning of knowledge went on throughout the trial. Finally the jury considered it and the Court instructed the jury in that case, in this context, having knowledge of the hazardous conditions means that the company knew or should have known of the hazardous condition. The jury convicted. The corporation was fined 450.000 dollars. The United States district judge affirmed the conviction and the case was appeared to the United States Court of Appeals. I cite in my outline at some length excerpts from the Court of Appeal's opinion. Judge Frank Easterbrook writing for the Court held: "Thus the jury instruction in this case equated a wilfulness with knowledge watered down knowledge to recklessness, defined recklessness as negligence, and used the civil rather than the criminal approach to negligence. Knowledge in the statute means actual knowledge. No case of which we are aware treats what a person should have known as knowledge or wilfulness, unless knowledge, recklessness criminal negligence and civil negligence are to merge into a single and mental state, it is essential to preserve the difference. What the amicus has done is he has taken and converted Rule 77 from a wilful and knowing mens rea to the mens rea for simple negligence. And so even under that standard there are no facts in the amicus report even suggesting that they should have known he was a Prosecution witness, and of greater importance, what difference does it make? If he's a Prosecution witness or not a Prosecution witness, if he's someone who knows something and a lawyer doesn't interview him, the lawyer is rendering ineffective representation of counsel. Even had the lawyers known in September that the witness was on the Prosecution's list, it was proper for them to interview the witness. Neither party in criminal litigation has a property interest in a witness. Each party has an obligation to his client to interview all persons who may have knowledge of the events upon which an indictment is based. Even had the attorneys in December asked substantive questions, that is, questions about the facts of 1992 in Kotor Varos, their conduct would not have been improper. Even if they had asked the same substantive questions in December that they asked in September, their conduct would not have been improper. The recollections and attitudes of witnesses change. Witnesses do not always tell the same story twice in the same way. Witnesses who have a few months to think about what they have said may say it differently the second time. An attorney has no assurance that when a person declines to be a witness that that declination is etched into stone. Witnesses change their mind. Witnesses talk with their friends. Witnesses think about things. No attorney should assume that once having gotten a refusal from a witness, that he or she should not try again. I submit most respectfully, Your Honour, that no order to show cause should be issued; that not contempt proceeding should be initiated; that this Court reach conclusions of law that will permit the reinstatement of Ms. Maglov as co-counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. I ask the Court to formulate conclusions of law so that when lawyers are appointed by the Registrar to represent indigent defendants before this Tribunal, these lawyers can look to your opinion in this cause and know that if they engage in honourable and honest but aggressive and tenacious representation, that this Tribunal will protect them. You have the fate of not only lawyers, Your Honour; you have the fate of defendants and their right to vigorous representation in your hands. And that's why I'm before you, because the issues that are raised by the Registrar transcend Ms. Maglov and affect all of us. Thank you very much -- thank you for indulging me. Thank you for letting me appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Second of all, I don't contest and didn't that the Prosecutor sent this material to whomever she sent it to, Mr. Ackerman or whoever, in April 2001. Should lawyers going to a community search through all of their files and all of their -- all of the materials they've received in discovery and ascertain the names of witnesses in that community who appear on the Prosecution's list? Probably. That would be good lawyering. I don't dispute that. She's not charged with bad lawyering. She's not charged -- she's not charged with anything at this point. But in any event, the assertions aren't that she didn't conduct a pre-trial preparation in the way the Court might do so or the Tribunal might do so or counsel might do so or the way my learned friend would. It's -- it's a question -- it's a question, Your Honours, of whether or not the interviewing of the witness Ms. Maglov conducted herself improperly. I think my learned colleague has misconstrued my position vis-a-vis the amicus. I am not levelling charges against the amicus; of course not. I am saying with all deference that his interpretation of the mens rea required for Rule 77 is not consistent with the case law, with the common law, with the experience of the common law courts. I am suggesting that his interpretation is not the interpretation that I want this Court to accept. This does not constitute levelling charges. This constitutes an intellectual disagreement on the concept of a mental state. At least in the United States we do not characterise such intellectual differences as one party levelling charges against the other. They may do so in the jurisdictions in which my friend practices, but lawyers and judges frequently have differences in the jurisdictions in which I practice which do not rise to the level of irritation that levelling charges would suggest. Second of all, I certainly did not assume that the Court would not consider any matters that were -- any matters that were before it in this cause in considering whether it would initiate contempt proceedings. And under the rules, I think the Court can judicially notice the events in the area, the circumstances in the area. Of course. And I expected that it would do so. I just did not expect that I would argue these matters. And lastly, I did not quote Judge Hunt out of context. Yes, Judge Hunt was referring to witnesses who have direct knowledge of the defendant's involvement, but to have direct knowledge of someone who is vicariously charged as a co-conspirator, as a solicitor, as an aider and abettor is very different than having actual knowledge of the activities of a principle. And how do we know as lawyers who has direct knowledge and who does not? First, if we don't have the witness's statement or haven't read it, we go to the witness and ask the witness what the witness knows. He is the source. The witness is the font of our knowledge. If we have the witness's statement from the prosecution and believe, A, that the investigator who took the statement took a complete statement; B, that it was correctly translated; C, that it was transliterated back into English correctly; and that the interrogator did not limit or excise from the statement matters which were inconsistent with the Prosecutor's position, then perhaps we could rely on the statement to find out if a witness had direct knowledge. But not all investigators act with the level of integrity that's required. I think that even where you have a witness statement and the witness says, "I have no direct knowledge of your client," you still must interview him. You still must go and say, "You don't know. But who does know? Take me to somebody who can help me. Tell me what is said in the community. Tell me what you've heard about my client from others," for it may be that this Tribunal will consider such hearsay as probative evidence. That's the job of a lawyer, and that's what this Tribunal would have done in the circumstances in which Ms. Maglov found herself. We practice criminal law. Contempt is not knowing and wilful. It is not negligence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Shellow, during his submissions mentioned several facts and opened several doors that I should like to refer to in my brief submissions. The first of those questions is the status of the witness, that is, the way in which the status of the witness is described in the report. In the report, the status of the witness in connection with his protective status is mentioned in one place only, paragraph 7, under the heading "Analysis." And I should like to quote that part of the report. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... for full protection as the Prosecution witness." [Interpretation] In the report it is not mentioned anywhere that full protection was given to the witness; therefore, the status of the witness refers to his status as a Prosecution witness and not as a protected witness. Mr. Shellow also mentioned in the course of his presentation that in the documents on the basis of which the proceedings are conducted in this Tribunal, there is no rule that makes it incumbent upon counsel to introduce themselves to witnesses or to anyone else that they contact in the field. I should again like to quote in English Rule 18, paragraph 2 of the Code of Ethics of the Tribunal which specifically says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ... the unrepresented person of the role counsel plays in the matter, the persons right to counsel under the rules, and the nature of legal representation in general." [Interpretation] I understand this provision as implying the obligation of Defence counsel and all those taking part in the proceedings when contacting persons in the field to introduce themselves by first and last name and to indicate the profession or title or position they hold in this Tribunal. I should like to go back for a moment to the witness statement that has been attached to the report. There is no doubt that during the visit or visits to the witness, reference was made to whether -- to the point whether the witness would testify or not for the Defence. And then the witness was told, and not asked, about Brdjanin's guilt. In the last statement of the witness, in paragraph 4, last sentence, the witness was told, "You know that Mr. Brdjanin may be held responsible for the events in that municipality if his position was a position in the regional Crisis Staff." At the end of this sentence, there is a question mark, but this is a statement not a question and the witness is simply asked to confirm it, because that is the way it has been worded. This sentence, or rather, this statement or assertion in my opinion is an attempt to influence the witness to change his statement up to a point. I don't think that the fact that Ms. Maglov and Mr. Peric note that the witness did not know Mr. Brdjanin or anything about him. But as Mr. Shellow himself has said, he may change his position; he may remember certain facts. And this assertion addressed to the witness can influence him when he is making his statement. I should also like to remind Your Honours of Article 14 of the Code of Ethics which speaks about the integrity of evidence and the protection of evidence. So Defence counsel must constantly and at all times protect the integrity of evidence. I mention Article 14 in the context of Rule 5(A), and that is the Defence counsel must act professionally, attentively, with care, integrity, honesty, and belief, and faith. By presenting the names and profession and the place where the witness is employed to a person who has been described as person Z, in December 2000, Ms. Maglov and Mr. Peric did violate Article 5(A) in my opinion of the Code of Ethics that is applicable in this Tribunal and in connection with Article 14 of the same Code of Ethics. All these violations, in my submission, do affect the belief that Article 5(D) has been violated. Therefore, any conduct of a person appearing in this Tribunal which is not in accordance with the Code of Ethics does lead to the violation of the integrity of that person, in this case Defence counsel, and the integrity of the legal profession as a whole. Thank you.

utterances.text: And then address the other matter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: The statement -- the words are: "You know how Mr. Brdjanin can be responsible for events in Kotor Varos if his position was the president of the regional Crisis Staff." And the question is whether or not that statement was made with the inflection of the voice going up at the end and that became a question and that's why it was put with a question mark or whether the voice went down and that it should have had a period. I assume it had a question mark there because it was the intent of the person who translated it to demonstrate that it was a question and not an assertion. Now, secondly, let's -- let's even assume that it was -- that it was an affirmative statement. This is a statement made in September. They hadn't seen a Prosecutor's statement by that time -- they hadn't seen a statement given to the Prosecutor. And they go to a witness and they say basically -- you know, you go to a witness who supposedly witnessed a hold-up and you say, "How could you have seen that? It was dark outside." Now, are you telling the witness I want you to testify that you didn't see what you claim you saw? Of course not. That is, in questioning a witness, the subtleties of syntax in which the amicus would ask us to engage just is not appropriate. The questioning of a witness is a spontaneous, creative, imaginative act. We are trying to learn something from someone who may know something. Now, as far as -- as far as the amicus now going to Rule 18, which I had before me a moment ago, and Rule 14. Rule 18 -- no. These are Rules of Procedure. That's not what I want. And that's not what I want -- here, I have it. Rule 18, it says: "If counsel is dealing with a person who's not represented, you shouldn't give advice to an unrepresented person. And Ms. Maglov didn't. You might advise the witness to secure legal representation, but it's not required. And he must inform the unrepresented person of the role counsel plays. Well, she did at the beginning in September. And I doubt that she did it again in December. It doesn't say you must do so as the outset of the interview. And the person's right to counsel under the rules just wouldn't have been appropriate. You're not asking a witness to incriminate himself or herself. And the nature of legal representation in general is that the nature of legal representation by counsel or is that the nature of legal representation in an adversary system or in a civil system? I just don't know. That doesn't help matters any. That doesn't help to clarify 5(A) and (D). And as far as article 14 is concerned, "Counsel must at all times maintain the integrity of evidence whether it is written, oral, or any other form, which is or may be submitted to the Tribunal." That is what at least in the United States is referred to as the integrity or chain of custody, of testimony of witnesses, that you don't destroy documents, that you don't write on documents that you're not supposed to. That doesn't address the question of how you question a person who may have knowledge of events. That has nothing to do with that. If what the -- if what the amicus is suggesting is that Ms. Maglov suborned perjury, that's something else again entirely, but it certainly isn't in this record. Now I would like to address very briefly the Court's question of misconduct in contempt. It is the position of counsel and Ms. Maglov that contempt falls basically into two categories: Acts that are committed before the Court and acts that are committed out of court. For acts that are committed out of court - to be contempt - there must be a wilful and intentional violation of a court -- of an explicit court order in that case or a general order of the court applying to all cases or a wilful and intentional violation of a serious provision of the Code of Professional Conduct. That is a provision that is intended to preserve the integrity of the Court and the administration of justice. It is not every misconduct out of court that constitutes contempt. Would it have been better for Ms. Maglov at the outset of the first interview, before there was any social conversation with the witness, for her to say, "I am a Defence counsel of Mr. Brdjanin"? Perhaps. But there's no explicit command that it must be done at the outset. It's just that at some point it should be done. And she did it. Should she in December have repeated the identification? I would have. Probably the Court -- the Tribunal would have. But you don't have to tell a person twice who you are and what you're doing there. Should she have phrased her questions differently? I don't think so. She acted like a lawyer. She acted like we expect lawyers to act. There is nothing in Rule 14, 18, 5 that says she acted improperly. No. Misconduct out of court should be in a whole variety of ways. You can tell a newspaper that in your opinion a witness was drunk when he was on the stand. That's misconduct. If the witness has already testified and there's no trier of fact who's going to be contaminated, it may not be such a serious matter. And so misconduct to rise to the level of contempt -- contempt carries with it, Your Honours, the meaning of the word -- "contempt" in the English language, the etymology of "contempt" is that what you are doing is you are acting -- it's the same root as "contemptuous," as "contemptible." It's a very bad thing that you that do it intentionally and knowingly and wilfully, that you're trying -- you're trying to obstruct the proceedings, the administration, justice. That's the kind of misconduct in which one must engage for a Court to bring an orderly show of cause why a witness -- why a lawyer must be held in contempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I have two kinds of questions to amicus curiae. The first one concerns disclosure of witness's statement. utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not investigate how and when the witness statement was delivered to Mr. Ackerman as lead counsel. As for how and when the statement was disclosed to Ms. Maglov, according to what she stated, they received the statement in between the two visits in September and December. This is what she says in her statement, and this was confirmed by Mr. Peric. So my submission is that the actual knowledge by Ms. Maglov and Mr. Peric of the witness statement has even greater weight because they went to see the witness again in December and again raised the question of his testimony. Also, they disclosed the name and surname of the witness to Mr. Z, who has nothing to do with this case, which I also consider to be a violation of the Code of Ethics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question concerns non-Serbs who might be approached by Mrs. Maglov in Kotor Varos. According to your investigation in the municipality of Kotor Varos, are there any other non-Serb person who was approached by Mrs. Maglov to become a witness for the Defence counsel in Brdjanin and Talic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from Ms. Maglov's statement and those of Mr. Peric and [redacted] [redacted], he advised them to contact another person of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We will have to redact again -- yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- [redacted]. Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I forgot something that I had taken up with my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let -- let the amicus finish first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I'll give you the floor. Sorry to have interrupted you, Mr. Ukropina. You said: "Your Honour, from Ms. Maglov's statement and those of Mr. Peric and --" the gentleman whose name we have struck off now "-- he advised them to contact another person of Croat ethnicity."

utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you were going to say something else. I don't know. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. UKROPINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. But there's no trace as to whether they did contact that other person, whether they interviewed him and whether that person has been put on the list of Defence witnesses or not. But I -- what I would also like to point out is the document appointing the amicus and giving instructions to the amicus as to what he should do. And as far as I was able to understand those instructions, especially whether there are any other non-Serbs that might testify in this case, it was not covered by those instructions and, therefore, I did not investigate the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Shellow, do you have any final -- a final remark that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: Only an administrative matter that I discussed with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: The document which I have designated as an outline which has been submitted to the interpreter and I believe either will be or has been already submitted to the report - and a copy of it, I believe, has been tendered to counsel for the Prosecution - contains the information that the Tribunal has redacted from the statements that we have made. And so I would ask then that it be filed with the Court and filed under seal. And that will give the Court the benefit of the authorities upon which I'm relying, the benefit to some extent of my attempts at argument therein. It's essentially an outline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can bypass that very easily, not having it admitted as an official document. It's just a document that has been circulated which the -- we will take as an aid to what we have in the transcript and to the personal notes that we have taken. And the same applies to Ms. Korner and the other officials of this court. So in other words, it will be a document which we will use obviously but not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHELLOW
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for bringing this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to Judge Taya's questions. We can supply -- clearly, we were just asked for the date; I mean, nothing further. But we can supply the documentation in relation to that delivery if it's so required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mentioned a receipt earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We give -- the Defence counsel are always asked to sign receipts. Your Honours may have noticed that Mr. Ackerman never seems to have any papers, although Madam Fauveau does. And so he's stopped signing those receipts now. But in those days I think he was still signing them. So we do have receipts. And I think the situation has been with Mr. Ackerman on some occasions he's collected the documents from the locker and on some, as Judge Taya rightly says, we've sent it over by DHL. But it shouldn't be too difficult to find out which -- which type of delivery this one was. So Your Honours, we're simply saying if Your Honours at some later stage would require that information, we can provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I can safely say yes, we will require that information. And you have our authority to file it -- to file the information formally, with a copy to be transmitted to Ms. Maglov and her counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything that you would like to say, Mr. Brdjanin? I don't suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the lawyers, I really think anything from me would be superfluous. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that brings us to the end of today's hearing. I wish to thank you, Mr. Shellow, for having come over and for having given us such high-level argumentation on the subject. We will await for the further notes of submission and we will come down with our -- hand down with our judgement -- our decision in due course, keeping in mind that none of us will be present here in August but we'll -- we'll be working on it in cooperation with the staff that will be here during the month of August. But as soon as practicable, we will try and hand down our decision. I thank you, Ms. Korner, also for your assistance. And to you, in particular, Mr. Ukropina, for your report and also for your patience and assistance today. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Brdjanin, for coming.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.28 p.m.
